passage:
Monday. Damini watched Ms Varghese hand back the spelling test. “Kabir got six right, up from two,” the teacher said. “That is real work.” Kabir sat up straight.
Wednesday. A boy copied the way Lalremsiami counted on fingers under the desk, and a few children giggled. The teacher put down her chalk. “In this room nobody laughs at how somebody works things out. Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch.” Lalremsiami counted again, openly this time, and got the sum right. The giggling boy went red and looked at his desk.
Friday. Another child got a sum wrong. Damini heard the girl next to her whisper, “Good try, look, you're nearly there.” The teacher, at the board, did not turn around, but she smiled.

qa.q: On which day did the teacher stop the giggling?
qa.a: On Wednesday the teacher stopped the giggling after a boy copied how Lalremsiami counted on fingers.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when the teacher said, “Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch”?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt protected but still exposed, since Lalremsiami counted again in front of everyone after being mocked, and the room then watched.

qa.q: What small choice by the teacher on Wednesday did the most to change the room?
qa.a: Stopping the mockery straight away, and then asking Lalremsiami to show the method, so that the child who was laughed at was heard and not shamed further.

qa.q: What might Damini have noticed about how the teacher's habits spread by Friday?
qa.a: Damini noticed that a girl now whispered, “Good try,” to the child beside her after a wrong sum, the same effort-praising tone the teacher used, which shows children copy what the teacher does.

grounding: A teacher who praises effort, stops mockery quickly and applies the same rules to everyone sets a climate that children copy, seen by a pupil.

passage: “Come here, my little Zoya, and I'll tell you about Mr Anand,” said Nani Salma. “When I was ten, our teacher was Mr Anand, and our class had a girl called Meena who read very slowly. One day a boy began copying her, and the room laughed. Mr Anand did not shout. He walked to the back, stood beside Meena's desk and said, 'In this room everyone gets the time they need. Meena, please begin again.' We waited. Meena finished, red in the face, and he said, 'Thank you. Well read.' Next day my bench-mate Hafsa told a shy boy, 'Take your time.' I heard myself say it too. We had copied him without knowing.”

qa.q: Where did Mr Anand stand when he spoke to the class about Meena?
qa.a: Mr Anand stood beside Meena's desk at the back of the room.

qa.q: What might Meena have felt while the class waited for her to finish?
qa.a: Meena probably felt nervous and exposed but also supported, since Meena finished red in the face and was thanked for reading well.

qa.q: What could a teacher do today when a child is mocked for reading slowly?
qa.a: A teacher could stop it calmly, stand near the child, give the child time to read and thank them for it, as Mr Anand did.

qa.q: How might the boy who copied Meena have felt when the teacher spoke?
qa.a: The boy may have felt caught and ashamed, since the room stopped laughing and the teacher's calm words made the copying look unwelcome.

grounding: An elder remembers a teacher who stopped mockery calmly and treated everyone the same, and how the children copied his manner.
